claims.text: The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by the absence of nanoscale precipitates.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a single-phase, disordered solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has good plasticity and machinability.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has moderate or relatively low hardness and strength.
A suitable thermal treatment can induce nanoscale precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
A slight compositional adjustment can induce nanoscale precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
The induced precipitates may be ordered B2 or other intermetallic phases.
Nanoscale precipitates act as discrete barriers to dislocation motion.
The proposed precipitate strengthening occurs through Orowan looping.
Dislocations move relatively unhindered in the simple CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Finely distributed precipitates will increase the yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
Finely distributed precipitates will increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Precipitate strengthening will cause at most a modest reduction in ductility.
The proposed comparison uses an as-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi control and a heat-treated equimolar CoCrFeNiTi sample processed identically except for the thermal treatment.
The hypothesis is limited to room temperature through 600 °C under uniaxial compression or tensile loading at controlled strain rates.
The hypothesis may not apply when other mechanisms, such as extreme grain-boundary strengthening in nanocrystalline material, dominate the response.
Failure of samples containing verified nanoscale precipitates to show a statistically significant yield-strength and hardness increase would falsify the proposed strengthening explanation.
Failure of the selected treatment to produce nanoscale precipitates would by itself falsify the claim that precipitate absence governs the starting alloy's low strength.
